system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2130-11-10 08:10:00 to 2130-11-13 12:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for his second maintenance cycle of high-dose methotrexate for primary central nervous system lymphoma. He had previously completed induction therapy and the first maintenance dose without complications. During this admission, he received high-dose methotrexate on day one, with leucovorin rescue initiated 24 hours later and continued until methotrexate levels dropped to 0.02, at which point it was discontinued. He developed mild, transient transaminitis and a drug-induced headache, both managed supportively. Constipation and cerumen impaction recurred but resolved with standard treatment. Aspirin and omeprazole were held during hospitalization and restarted at discharge. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans to continue outpatient chemotherapy as scheduled.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Hodgkin's disease, unspecified type, intrathoracic lymph nodes
Drug induced headache, not elsewhere classified
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MR HEAD W AND W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  The requisition states ___ year old man with metastatic melanoma
post cyberknife to right parietal resection bed. New dysmetria, ataxia."
However, according to the note by neuro-oncologist Dr. ___ in the ___
medical record dated ___, the patient has history of mixed
Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, status post brain biopsy in ___, and
s/p chemotherapy, now with dizziness and gait disturbance.

TECHNIQUE:  Sagittal T1 weighted, and axial T1 weighted, T2 weighted, FLAIR,
gradient echo, and diffusion-weighted images of the brain were obtained.
Following intravenous gadolinium administration, multiplanar T1 weighted
images of the brain were obtained.

COMPARISON:  ___ brain MRI with and without contrast, which also
states history of Hodgkin's and diffuse large cell composite lymphoma in the
requisition.

FINDINGS: 

The lesion extending from the posterior limb of the left external capsule into
the left cerebral peduncle of the midbrain demonstrates stable high T2 signal
without any residual contrast enhancement, and stable high signal on diffusion
tracer images without a correlate on the ADC map.  Multiple other, smaller
foci of high T2 signal in the subcortical, deep, and periventricular white
matter of the cerebral hemispheres are stable without contrast-enhancement. 
No new enhancing lesions are seen.

Linear susceptibility artifact is again seen in the posterior left frontal
lobe with the vertex, likely related to prior biopsy.  The ventricles are
stable in size, with all components of the left lateral ventricle larger than
the right, which indicates congenital or developmental asymmetry.  There is no
acute infarction. Major arterial flow voids are grossly preserved.

There is a small mucous retention cyst in the right maxillary sinus. The left
mastoid is not pneumatized, as seen previously.

IMPRESSION:


1. No evidence for acute intracranial abnormalities.
2. The lesion extending from the posterior left internal capsule into the left
cerebral peduncle of the midbrain demonstrates stable extent of high T2 signal
without any residual contrast enhancement. Other, smaller foci of high T2
signal in the supratentorial white matter are also stable without contrast
enhancement.
3. No evidence of new enhancing lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your scheduled high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. How have you been feeling since your last treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’ve been doing pretty well—no headaches, no balance issues, and I’ve been walking every day. Just a little tired sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Any nausea, vision changes, or weakness in your arms or legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. My hands are steady, and I can read fine. No floaters or blurriness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll be giving you methotrexate today at a higher dose—8 grams per square meter—as part of your maintenance therapy. This is your third dose since reinduction, and overall your seventh cycle since the relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I remember. It’s been going smoothly so far. Is the plan the same as last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar. We’ll start the infusion this afternoon at 5 p.m. Before that, we’ll give you fluids and sodium bicarbonate to keep your urine alkaline, which helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin—when does that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start leucovorin 24 hours after the methotrexate finishes. It helps ‘rescue’ your healthy cells from the chemo’s side effects. We’ll keep giving it until your methotrexate levels drop low enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my regular meds—should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold your aspirin and omeprazole while you’re here. Aspirin can affect bleeding risk, and we use ranitidine instead of omeprazole during chemo to avoid interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had constipation before with this treatment—should I start the magnesium citrate now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you. If you haven’t had a bowel movement by tomorrow, we’ll give the magnesium citrate. Docusate will stay on as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again, Mr. Thompson. We just finished your methotrexate infusion. It went smoothly, no reactions. You’re now on sodium bicarbonate to keep your urine pH above 7.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I didn’t feel much during the infusion—just a little warm at one point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common and normal. We’ll keep an eye on your labs over the next few days, especially kidney function and liver enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver numbers were a bit high last time—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect some mild, temporary elevation. As long as it’s not severe, it resolves on its own. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are looking stable. Creatinine is 0.9, which is normal. Liver enzymes are up a bit—ALT 185, AST 172—but that’s expected and not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, so that’s just from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common, temporary side effect. We’ll keep monitoring. Also, you have a brain MRI scheduled today to check how the lymphoma is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I forgot about that. Is it safe with the chemo in my system?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfectly safe. It’s just images—we’re not using any additional drugs. It’s important to see if the lesions are stable or shrinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Thompson. I have the MRI results. Good news—the lesion in your brain is stable. No new areas of concern, and no contrast enhancement, which means no active tumor growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So the treatment is still working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The disease is under control. Because of this, your oncologist plans to space out your treatments to every other month from now on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds great—fewer hospital stays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll still keep a close eye on you. Your next eye exam is scheduled for next month, since you’ve had vitreous involvement before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll make sure to go. Any other follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue seeing your oncologist regularly. Your systemic lymphoma remains in remission—last PET scan was clear, and your blood work is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your methotrexate level is now 0.09, which is low enough that we can stop leucovorin today. That means you’re clearing the drug well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m almost ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. We’ll restart your aspirin and omeprazole before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been a bit constipated—haven’t had a bowel movement since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s give you the magnesium citrate now. It usually works within a few hours. We’ll keep the docusate going daily to help prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll take it as needed from now on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs are stable, and you’ve responded well to the magnesium citrate. We’re on track for discharge tomorrow around 10 a.m.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need another MRI soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. Your oncologist will schedule the next one in a few months. For now, we’re focused on recovery and spacing out your treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart and cholesterol? Should I keep doing anything special?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your coronary disease is stable. Keep taking aspirin daily as prescribed. For cholesterol, continue your diet and any medications your doctor recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do have occasional dizziness—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as it’s mild and not worsening, it’s likely related to your history of vertigo. But mention it at your next visit if it increases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. You’re doing well and ready for discharge. Your final labs are normal, and your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. What’s the plan after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your docusate daily and use magnesium citrate as needed for constipation. Restart aspirin and omeprazole today. Your next chemo is in two months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I develop any symptoms—like headaches or balance issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your oncologist right away. But based on your MRI, things are stable. You’ve tolerated this cycle well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. It was a pleasure. Take care, and we’ll see you in the clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any new symptoms? Headache, nausea, weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. A bit tired, but that’s normal for me after chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Keep resting and hydrating. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge instructions are ready. You’ll get a copy with all medications, follow-up appointments, and when to call the clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, no sick contacts, stay hydrated, and avoid NSAIDs while on aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No ibuprofen, plenty of water, and wash hands often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, just to confirm—my next chemo is in two months, not one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your MRI showed stable disease, they’re extending the interval to every other month. It’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful news. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—should I restart my cholesterol meds if I’m not on them now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if they were prescribed before, please continue them. Discuss with your primary doctor if you’re unsure.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for his third maintenance cycle of high-dose methotrexate following reinduction therapy for CNS lymphoma, marking his seventh cycle since relapse. The chemotherapy infusion was administered without complications, and he developed only mild, expected elevations in liver enzymes. Constipation, a recurring issue during treatment, was managed with magnesium citrate. A brain MRI showed stable disease with no new enhancing lesions, allowing for an extension of treatment intervals to every other month. Aspirin and omeprazole were held during hospitalization and restarted at discharge. He was discharged home in stable condition with a plan for ongoing outpatient follow-up.
